item.title: St. Louis Notes
item.description: Miscellaneous notes on St. Louis slang and customs, from pronouncing Carondelet to defining a hoosier
item.content:encoded:
St. Louis is a city with a lot of regional culture. Here are the notes I’ve taken.

Food#

I made the St. Louis Food Map to keep track of the restaurants, bars, and cafes I’ve found in the region. The map is sortable by cuisine type (pizza, BBQ, Thai, coffee, etc.) and I’ve added ratings to every place I’ve been.

View the directory for an interactive database.

My Favorite Food in St. Louis is my subjective list of favorite dishes.

Regional food#

See Regional Foods of St. Louis for toasted ravioli, gooey butter cake, slingers and of course, St. Louis-style Pizza.

The City-County Split#

Not long after moving to St. Louis, I realized people don’t say “city and suburbs” around here, they say “city and county”. I researched the St. Louis city and county divide and wrote The Great Divorce.

Cardinal counties#

You’ll hear West County, South County, and North County as a colloquial way to refer to areas within St. Louis County.

There is no “East County”, as that would be St. Louis City. However, the area east of the Mississippi River is also part of the Greater St. Louis region, and commonly referred to as “Metro East”. This includes East St. Louis, Belleville, O’Fallon, and a few others.

STL#

STL is a common abbreviation used all over the area to represent St. Louis.

The Delmar Divide#

Delmar Boulevard is an East-West street that cuts through the middle of St. Louis city, and it represents a dividing line known as The Delmar Divide. Everything north of Delmar is known as North City, and south of it is the Central Corridor and South City. It’s often described as a racial and economic divide as well as a geographic one, shaped by decades of redlining and segregation.

The Interactive St. Louis Vacancy Map demonstrates one of the stark divides that happens right along the line.

Brick and Architecture#

One thing to get used to in St. Louis is how red everything is. St. Louis was once the largest brick producer in the world, due to innovations in brickmaking combined with the abundance of clay in the region, and that legacy really shows all throughout the city. The site Built St. Louis is an incredible resource for everything architecture and history related.

Many homes throughout the city are early 20th century brick-built homes, and entire historic neighborhoods are preserved in this style, such as Shaw and Lafayette Square.

Walkable#

St. Louis is not the most walkable city, but all the areas I’ve discovered that have walkable points of interest have been documented in Walkable Neighborhoods in St. Louis. STL Urbanists is a good source for other public transportation.

Business Districts#

I’ve carved out a spot in the map for major business districts of the area such as The Grove, Cherokee Street, and South Grand. You can read more at Where Is Dogtown? Mapping Local Names in St. Louis.

Biking#

On the STL Urbanists website, you can find a Safe Bike Route Map. They also have a public transportation map.

Free Attractions#

St. Louis actually has an impressive amount of free amenities, especially relative to other mid-sized cities.

The St. Louis Zoo is the most apparent example of this: a world-class zoo that holds its own against any other free or paid zoo. The Art Museum, Missouri History Museum, and Science Center are all free any day of the week, not just once a month on a Tuesday. It’s cool that there are so many things to do and they’re not price prohibitive.

Parks#

One of the biggest draws of St. Louis is all the green space. Forest Park is one of the largest city parks in America, and contains everything from the zoo and museums to outdoor amphitheaters and golf courses. Tower Grove Park is more of a local neighborhood park that hosts a farmer’s market and community events.

Language#

Street name pronunciations#

Although many of the streets in St. Louis have French sounding names, there are St. Louis-specific pronunciations for them that are not obvious.

There is a specific regional dialect of French known as Missouri French (or Paw-Paw French) that these pronunciations have been derived from.

  • Carondelet - kuh-RON-duh-let
  • Chouteau - SHOW-doe
  • Creve Coeur - kreev-core
  • Des Peres - duh-PAIR
  • Florissant - FLOR-uh-sent
  • Gravois - GRAV-oy
  • Laclede - luh-CLEED
  • Meramec - MER-uh-mack
  • Soulard - SOO-lard
  • DeBaliviere - duh-BAHL-a-ver
  • Bellefontaine - bell-fountain

Regional dialect#

  • “Muskacholi” - An endearing pronunciation for Mostaccioli used in St. Louis.
  • Warsh - Similar to the above, sometimes you’ll hear “warsh” instead of “wash” among an older generation.
  • Catty Corner - This is not entirely specific to the STL region, but people say catty corner here, whereas in the north it’s kitty corner. This data is substantiated in the Harvard dialect study.

St. Louis-isms#

  • The Lou - A popular nickname for St. Louis.
  • Hoosier - In the rest of the U.S., Hoosier refers to someone from Indiana, but in St. Louis it’s a pejorative term for a working class or rural person. A deeper dive found at St. Louis’ own language: hoosier on St. Louis City Talk.
  • Highway Farty - Highway 40 is part of Interstate 64, and many people still call it “Highway Farty” affectionately.
  • Jeffco - Jefferson County, the immediate county to the south of St. Louis County.

Local Customs#

Where did you go to high school?#

Frequently cited to be a common icebreaker for St. Louisans, the phrase “Where did you go to high school?” is used to suss out what socioeconomic circle a person belongs to, or perhaps to find shared acquaintances. No one has ever asked me this question, though.

Halloween#

In St. Louis, kids have to tell a joke to get treats on Halloween, which is one of my favorite local customs.

Golf carts#

People drive golf carts all around the St. Louis area. According to The Hill neighborhood, golf carts are allowed on Missouri streets, which explains why it’s so common here.

Candy Cane Lane#

A street in St. Louis Hills that goes all out during Christmas.

Art Hill#

Sledding on Art Hill in Forest Park is a common wintertime activity in St. Louis.

Brands#

There are a lot of regional products you’ll see around in St. Louis. Imo’s is the biggest local pizza chain, with Cecil Whittaker’s being the smaller pizza chain. Fitz’s is a local craft root beer, Vess is a popular cheap soda option, and Red Hot Riplets are the local potato chip brand.

St. Louis Bread Co. is widely known as Panera outside of the region, though some locals have eschewed it since it was acquired by private equity.

item.title: Regional Foods of St. Louis
item.description: An inventory of the specialty food of St. Louis, from gooey butter cake to gooey Provel cheese
item.content:encoded:
Most cities are lucky to have one local food speciality they can lay claim to, but St. Louis has an abundance of them. I’ve been interested to discover the food items that either originated in St. Louis or can only be found here.

So here’s what I’ve discovered so far:

St. Louis-style pizza#

A pizza style that is the standard all across the St. Louis region, consisting of a cracker-thin crust, a sweet, thick tomato sauce, and gooey Provel cheese.

See St. Louis-style Pizza for the full writeup.

My personal favorites for St. Louis-style pizza are Farotto’s, Faraci’s, and Pirrone’s.

Provel cheese#

The cheese of choice in St. Louis, Provel is an option in almost every pizza place and sandwich shop around the city. It’s a processed cheese product made of cheddar, provolone, and Swiss cheese, all mixed together with a hint of liquid smoke. It’s the ingredient that makes St. Louis-style pizza controversial, with its goopy texture and smoky, funky flavor.

Although it’s notable for its low melting point and unique texture it adds to pizza, you’ll also find it liberally applied to most house salads in Italian restaurants across the city.

St. Louis salad#

I don’t think you’ll find this on any other list of local St. Louis cuisine, but I can tell you that the house salad served in many restaurants in STL is unique to the region. The lettuce, tomato, and onion are standard salad ingredients, but the Italian dressing is sweet, almost candy like, and the salad is liberally covered in Provel cheese. Some places have so much Provel on top of the salad that you can hardly see a piece of lettuce poking out.

I do enjoy this salad, but I don’t feel very healthy after eating it.

BBQ & Meats#

There are two things to discuss here - St. Louis-style BBQ, and St. Louis cut ribs.

Ribs#

There’s a popular cut of ribs called a “St. Louis cut”, which is a spare rib with the ends neatly trimmed, resulting in a rectangular shape. This allows for even cooking, as you don’t have one end that is significantly wider than the other. Surprisingly, most BBQ spots around here don’t tend to use this cut.

It’s not exactly a style of regional food, but it’s worth mentioning.

BBQ#

BBQ in St. Louis is another contentious topic, with many arguing about what the style is and if it exists at all. Some say St. Louis-style is a mix between Kansas City BBQ and Memphis BBQ.

Here’s what I’ve observed: I’ve been to around a dozen BBQ spots in St. Louis so far, and I can say pork is king here. Pappy’s is the most famous for their ribs, and it’s well deserved. You’ll see pork steak on the menu at Beast BBQ, and most backyard BBQs. I would recommend against getting brisket, particularly if you’re a fan of Texas brisket, as the style is not really found here. (O’B’Que’s in Chesterfield is the closest I’ve found.)

I’ve heard it said that St. Louisans consume the most amount of BBQ sauce per capita, which tracks with the BBQ style. Ribs, pork steaks, and even backyard grilled hot dogs are slathered in sweet BBQ sauce. Pappy’s makes a Sweet Jane BBQ, which goes great on pulled pork or smoked chicken, and Maull’s is a classic BBQ sauce from the region. I’m partial to Freddie Lee’s Ghetto sauce.

I have also found that the smoked wings are slept on - they’re crisp and juicy and have been my favorite thing on the menu at several spots. Some places also have their own specialties, like the smoked salami at Adam’s Smokehouse.

As a lover of spicy vinegar-based BBQ sauce and wood-smoked savory meats, St. Louis-style is not my preferred style of BBQ, but if you stick to ribs and wings you’ll have a good time. It’s exciting that a BBQ scene exists here, and I’m looking forward to continuing to try more.

Where I’ve been so far#

  • O’B’Que’s
  • The Stellar Hog
  • Pappy’s Smokehouse
  • Dalie's Smokehouse
  • Beast Craft BBQ Co.
  • Adam’s Smokehouse
  • Salt & Smoke BBQ
  • Sugarfire Smokehouse
  • Bandana’s Bar-B-Q
  • Fourth City BBQ
  • The Shaved Duck (rip)

Pork steak#

Pork steak is a cut of meat derived from sliced pork butt, usually with the bone in. Often they’re grilled over high heat then slathered in BBQ sauce and braised until tender. Although most BBQ spots in St. Louis won’t have it on the menu, pork steak is known to all. It’s one of the primary meats of choice for any backyard BBQ.

Bar & Diner Food#

Toasted ravioli#

You’d be hard pressed to find a bar or restaurant in the entire St. Louis metro area that doesn’t serve toasted ravioli, also known as “t-ravs”. They’re the default appetizer of choice throughout the region - little beef-filled ravioli that are deep fried, sprinkled with parmesan, and served with marinara sauce for dipping.

I was a bit thrown off by toasted ravioli when I first moved here, as I always expect ravioli to be filled with ricotta cheese, not a smooth beef paste, but I got used to it. I tend to prefer the ones that are filled with something else, like the buffalo chicken t-ravs from Stacked, or the burnt end t-ravs from Salt & Smoke, or even the spinach artichoke t-ravs at McGurk’s.

The best t-ravs I’ve had so far are made at Bud’s Pizza and Beer.

Trashed wings#

Trashed wings are a double-fried style of bar wings. First the wings are fried, then tossed in sauce and fried again, caramelizing the sauce and making them twice as crisp.

Slinger#

A slinger is a greasy spoon diner meal that consists of eggs, hash browns and a hamburger patty, covered in chili and cheese. I haven’t been drunk enough to ever need this meal, but I’m sure I’ll be exposed to it eventually.

Brain sandwich#

Yeah…St. Louis is one of the only places in the U.S. you can still get a brain sandwich. You can get it at Schottzie’s Bar & Grill, deep-fried and served on marble rye with pickles and mustard.

Chinese#

St. Louis fried rice#

St. Louis, particularly the north side of St. Louis city, is home to many old style chop suey shops serving up a particular variation of fried rice that is much darker than your average fried rice. I’m not sure if it’s just extra soy sauce or any other particular ingredients that are used. An STLPR article about it: From Far East to Midwest: chop suey’s last stand.

St. Paul sandwich#

I have yet to try this delicacy, but chop suey shops all around St. Louis have it on the menu. It consists of a fried egg foo young patty between two slices of white bread, with lettuce and mayonnaise. It’s an interesting historical fusion of flavors, and I’m happy to see it lives on in the present day.

Hot Braised Chicken#

I haven’t been able to find out too much about this dish and what makes it special, but you’ll see it on many restaurants all over the St. Louis region, and basically nowhere else. It seems to me kind of similar to sweet and sour chicken style, but tossed in General Tso-style sauce.

Desserts#

Gooey butter cake#

The signature dessert of St. Louis, gooey butter cake is a dense, sticky, rich cake with a crisp, flaky top layer. It almost has the consistency of a light brownie, or a lemon bar without any lemon. You’ll find them in many cafes alongside the croissants and muffins.

The consistency can vary a lot from recipe to recipe, and I like it when there are contrasting textures between the rich, gooey center and the flaky crust, like a pie. Sometimes the whole thing has one unified texture, and it loses its appeal for me.

Frozen custard/concrete#

Ted Drewes Frozen Custard has been a St. Louis institution since 1929. They began the concept of the concrete, a frozen custard with mix-ins, which was later co-opted by Dairy Queen, which they called blizzards.

A popular St. Louis tradition is to get Ted Drewes during Christmastime then walk down the streets of Candy Cane Lane, a neighborhood where every house is all done up with Christmas lights.

Snacks#

Red Hot Riplets#

Red Hot Riplets are a brand of ridged chips with a unique sweet BBQ and cayenne flavor. In addition to just being a chip, you’ll find Red Hot Riplet flavor and spice blend used often. Imo’s tosses their fried wings in Red Hot Riplet seasoning as a dry rub. I’m generally not a fan of BBQ chips, but I do enjoy the Riplet rub on wings.

Tzitzel bagel#

A cornmeal-coated bagel, which originated in Pratzel’s Bakery in the early 1900s. You can still find this at Lefty’s Bagels and Baked & Boiled. You can read more about tzitzel at The tzitzel bagel — a crunchy St. Louis classic with a century-old story.

Closing Thoughts#

Flavor profile#

One thing I’ve noticed across the board is that the main flavor profile in St. Louis is sweet. The signature BBQ sauce is sweet, the pizza sauce is sweet, the salad dressing is sweet, and the desserts are extra sweet. Vinegary, sour, or bitter flavors are not a big part of the regional palette.

Other things of note#

St. Louis is home to one of the largest Bosnian populations in the U.S. and as a result, there are a fair amount of Bosnian and Balkan restaurants - notably Balkan Treat Box and a strip of restaurants in the Bevo Mill neighborhood.

item.title: St. Louis-style Pizza
item.description: Discovering, explaining, and ranking St. Louis's unique regional pizza style
item.content:encoded:
St. Louis-style pizza is a regional variation of pizza that is ubiquitous across the entire St. Louis metro area. For many, the pizza style is synonymous with Imo’s, a local chain that has locations in all the far reaches of Missouri and southern Illinois, but many local pizza places all around St. Louis make their own variation of this unique pizza style.

Although divisive, St. Louis-style pizza has fervent defenders (I reference two independent articles in this post that start with “In Defense of…”). I personally had never heard of St. Louis-style pizza until I moved here, and was intrigued to discover hundreds of restaurants and bars serving them up (Imo’s alone has over 100!).

My first experiences with STL-style pizza were not the best, and initially I was the classic dismissive transplant, but over time I’ve acquired a taste and appreciation for this regional specialty. For every birthday, graduation, and celebration, St. Louis-style pizza is there for us, and I can see why so many people feel so deeply protective of it.

My Rankings#

Here’s a subjective rated list of the places I’ve tried. I would say the top three or four are all vying for first place at the moment.

  1. Faraci Pizza - Rectangular pizza, sliced provel, and a crispy, yeasty crust.
  2. Bono’s Pizzeria: Crispy, thin, tavern-esque pizza with light sauce and Provel.
  3. Farotto’s - A pizza with extra-extra-thin buttery, flaky crust, a slightly sweet sauce, and quality ingredients. Just don’t get Jimmy’s favorite (shrimp and bacon…why??). This is my place of choice to take out of town visitors, as the rest of the food is also great.
  4. Pirrone’s Pizzeria - It’s a bit out of the way from the city itself, but worth a visit. Pirrone’s makes a rectangular pizza with a crispy, buttery crust, where the cheese and sauce blend to make an orange mix.
  5. Salvage Yard - A solid choice for a standard STL-style.
  6. Imo’s Pizza - By far the most famous and infamous pizza in town, Imo’s is THE St. Louis pizza chain and the only STL-style many people have ever tried. Imo’s has a mass-produced flavor to it, unlike the home-style vibes of a lot of other spots. The quality also varies a lot from location to location. It can be okay, but not the best representation of pizza in the area, in my opinion. Sometimes I do specifically crave an Imo’s pizza, though.
  7. Failoni’s - A brick-oven pizza with a very crisp cracker-like crust. (I believe this also counts as Uncle Leo’s pizza, as they’re under the same ownership, but I haven’t tried it to confirm.)
  8. Nick & Elena’s - I know people love this place, and the old-school vibes are top-notch, but I didn’t personally like the pizza (specifically the sauce was way too sweet for me).
  9. Cecil Whittaker’s - This was one of my least favorite St. Louis-style pizzas I’ve tried.
  10. Elicia’s Pizza - The first St. Louis-style pizza I ever tried was from Elicia’s. It was completely burnt and inedible, and unfortunately they’re no longer in business for me to know whether or not that was a fluke.

You can vote for your own favorites on each page! I’d love to see how my rankings compare with the community’s.

So I’ve tried a variety of fan favorites around the city, but I’m always open to new suggestions. A few I have yet to try are Affton Pizza Company, Angelo’s, Kevin’s Place, and plenty more.

What is an STL-style Pizza?#

Cheese#

You can’t talk about St. Louis-style pizza without talking about Provel - it’s the most unique and controversial aspect of the pizza. Provel is made up of cheddar, Swiss, and provolone cheese with a hint of liquid smoke, and it’s processed and emulsified like American cheese. I would say it tastes kind of similar to a smoked gouda with the consistency of American cheese (those who did not grow up with it often describe it as plasticky). Provel was developed in the ’40s as an answer to the cheese pull issue, to ensure slices could be cut and removed easily. With Provel, you can’t end up accidentally pulling off all the cheese on a slice with a single bite, so I can understand the rationale.

Pizza generally consists of three ingredients (crust, sauce, and cheese) and most styles of pizza default to mozzarella. Provel being so different in both flavor and consistency from what anyone outside of the region expects is, in my opinion, what throws people off so much when they try it for the first time.

I’ve had dozens of STL-style pizzas at this point (see my ratings below) so I know what to expect, but I will admit the first time I was genuinely confused about what I was experiencing and it has been an acquired taste. If you grew up with Provel, however, that would be a different story, and you’d already be used to the taste and have years of fond memories associated with it.

But the truth is that my love for Provel is intense, almost mystical, and I’ve finally started taking it seriously.

Adam Rothbarth, In Defense of a St. Louis Favorite, Provel Cheese

Crust#

One thing all St. Louis-style pizzas have in common is the crust is very thin. Some describe it as unleavened, but usually the dough is made with a light amount of yeast and low hydration, resulting in that cracker-thin crisp. In Kenji López-Alt’s famous dissertation, he describes it as a pizza nacho, which is definitely an interesting and not entirely inaccurate description.

And yet, ever since tasting it for the first time, I haven’t been able to stop thinking about it. And I’ve finally figured out why I love it so much. St. Louis-style pizza is not pizza. It’s a big, pizza-flavored nacho.

J. Kenji López-Alt, In Defense of St. Louis-Style Pizza

This article was in fact the first step for me towards seeing this pizza from another angle.

Sauce#

The sauce on a St. Louis-style pizza is also unique. In general, it’s significantly sweeter and thicker than your standard pizza sauce. Some recipes, like Imo’s, even use straight tomato paste as opposed to whole tomatoes. The sweetness can vary, with some places almost tasting like a tomato jam to me.

Cut#

St. Louis-style pizza, like other Midwest styles of pizza, is cut into squares, resulting in some pieces having an edge, some being all middle-piece, and some being extra-crispy corner pieces. I’ve never liked the corner pieces much, but they seem to be everyone’s favorite. Cutting a STL-style pizza into triangles would just feel wrong.

Toppings#

You’ll see all the standard toppings on a STL-style. It’s important that the sausage should be bulk sausage placed on the pizza raw, not pre-cooked sausage bits like you’ll see at national chain pizza spots. I don’t know why, but I’ve also seen a lot of shrimp as a topping here which I’ve never seen anywhere else (not a fan), and if you get bacon on your pizza, it’s in the form of whole strips as opposed to bacon bits (am a fan).

Tavern-style Controversy#

Not so long ago, the term “tavern style” came into popularity, generally referring to the thin-crust style of pizza commonly served in bars and taverns across the Chicagoland area. This was seen as unfair in the eyes of many St. Louisans, as Chicago already has a regional variation of pizza in deep dish, and St. Louisans have been eating thin pizzas cut into squares for decades.

There are many regions of the midwest that all lay claim to the thin pizza cut into squares. Milwaukee and Chicago claim to have invented the concept. Columbus, Ohio has a version with an extreme amount of toppings layered edge-to-edge. Tombstone frozen pizzas was started in Wisconsin in the early ’60s, clearly a style of pizza that fits the “tavern-style” description.

Personally, I choose to think of it all as Midwestern-style pizza with regional variations. Only St. Louis does Provel cheese, and every single place that I’ve ever seen calling their pizza St. Louis-style has Provel on it or a Provel blend, so I would consider that the most essential difference. I also find the crust to be much thinner and more cracker-like than all the Chicago thin-crust pizzas I’ve eaten throughout my life.

I think St. Louis has their own thing going here and it’s pretty cool that something so unique and special can be found all over this region and almost nowhere else.

Regional Sub-variations#

Even within St. Louis-style pizza, there are sub-variations.

North#

I’ve noticed pizzas like Pirrone’s, Faraci’s, and Angelo’s, which are found on the north side of the St. Louis area, are all similar in a specific way. They’re rectangular, have a slightly thicker, yeastier crust, and the cheese and sauce blend together to make an orange hue.

South#

Meanwhile, Failoni’s and the original Imo’s are based on the south side of the St. Louis area, and the pizza are round, with a flatter, thinner crust, and the cheese is clearly a separate layer on top of the sauce.

This might not be entirely accurate, and most places do the round pizza, but I think it’s interesting to note.

Making a Pizza from Scratch#

Loosely based on a recipe posted on reddit by HouseofProvel, I made a St. Louis-style pizza from scratch with a three-day ferment on the crust. I opted to use slices of Provel as opposed to shredded as it’s the way Faraci’s does it.

I thought it came out pretty good, though I’d make some changes if I do it again. I made the crust with butter because I like butter, but shortening would be better for a crispier, lighter crust. I’d add slightly more sweetness to the sauce, and I’d use a little more yeast in the crust.

What Do I Think?#

I like pizza. I think (almost) all pizza is good. I love trying new things, especially regional food that you can’t get everywhere. My personal favorite styles of pizza are thick, bready styles, like Sicilian, Detroit-style and pan pizza. I’m also a fan of fresh, high-quality ingredients, like the fresh basil and mozzarella found on a Neapolitan margherita pizza.

So personally, St. Louis-style or even Chicago thin-crust are just never going to be on the top of my list, because I’m here for the dough. Nonetheless, I still like it and have acquired the taste since moving here, and I’m still excited to try all the spots and decide which one is my favorite. Sometimes I specifically crave a St. Louis-style pizza, and I’d miss it if I no longer lived here.

But most of my favorite pizzas around the city are not specifically St. Louis-style.

Other Pizza in St. Louis#

Although St. Louis-style pizza is obviously the most common style to be found in the region, there’s also New York-style at La Pizza, Detroit style at Nicky Slices, Chicago thin-crust at J.J. Twig’s, Neapolitan style at Fordo’s Killer Pizza, standard pizza at Bud’s Pizza and Beer, and many more found all around the city. I have yet to try a Sicilian-style or deep dish in St. Louis, but I’m looking forward to continuing my pizza journey.

item.title: The Great Divorce
item.description: How one fateful decision has divided the St. Louis region for 150 years
item.content:encoded:
Did you know St. Louis was almost the capital of the U.S.? At its peak, it was the 4th largest city in the country, booming in population and industry, and big enough that by 1904 it hosted the Olympics and the World’s Fair in the same year.

Many factors have contributed to the city’s population decline over the following decades - white flight, highway development, redlining, and the economy shifting away from the river - from more than 850,000 residents in the 1950s to less than 300,000 now. One persistent structural issue underlying these events is the city-county split known as “The Great Divorce”.

A City Divided#

The City of St. Louis voted to separate from St. Louis County in 1876, becoming one of the few independent cities in America. Most other cities sit inside a county, like Chicago within Cook County, but St. Louis City and County are completely separate entities. This separation permanently froze the boundaries of St. Louis at 66 square miles**, which resulted in unforeseen consequences for the city.

St. Louis City and St. Louis County

Frozen borders#

Most other cities have continued to grow and expand over the last two hundred years - Chicago, for example, had dozens of annexations of its surrounding towns and villages between 1880 and now, during which it expanded from 36 square miles to 234 today. St. Louis remained at 66 square miles during that time.

If St. Louis had followed in the footsteps of other cities, it would have absorbed many of the surrounding areas like Clayton, Maplewood, Richmond Heights, Webster Groves, and Kirkwood, but instead those are all separate cities.

Population stagnation#

St. Louis City is not close to being in the top 150 largest cities by area, yet the Greater St. Louis area had the 21st highest population in the U.S. in 2020.

St. Louis City and County population from 1880 to 2020

The suburbs have rapidly expanded over this time period, but the city has stagnated. This disparity has had an effect on the city’s reputation.

The Most Dangerous City?#

In 2024, St. Louis had the highest murder rate of the 24 cities studied. But while parts of St. Louis are legitimately dangerous, this stat doesn’t tell the whole story. St. Louis City only represents 10% of the population of its metro area - in stark contrast to the nearly 30% that Chicago represents.

CityMetro pop.City pop.Share of metro
Chicago9,618,5022,746,38828%
St. Louis2,820,253301,57810%

City population as a share of its metro, 2020

Crime is reported by geographic boundary. Since St. Louis hasn’t expanded its borders in 150 years, its lower-crime suburbs fall outside the city borders and never enter the stats, so the rate reflects only the dense urban core, not the wider region.

Thought experiment#

If St. Louis City and County were to be one combined entity, what would the stats look like? I decided to add up the numbers to see how much of a difference it would make.

Measured across the city and county together, the homicide rate drops from 87 to 28 per 100k. Treating the combined STL City and County area as a single city is a bit contrived, but there are cities like San Antonio, Texas, which is a somewhat similarly sized city in both population and area.

PlaceLand areaPopulationHomicidesRate per 100k
St. Louis City62 sq. mi301,57826387
St. Louis County508 sq. mi1,004,12510410
St. Louis City + County570 sq. mi1,305,70336728
San Antonio499 sq. mi1,434,6251309

St. Louis City + County compared with San Antonio, 2020

Even in this hypothetical scenario, the crime stats are still above the national average (which the FBI estimated at 6.5 in 2020) but much lower than St. Louis City alone. Among the 296 cities over 100,000 that reported 2020 data to the FBI, St. Louis City had the highest murder rate in the nation - the combined city would instead rank roughly 15th, in the same range as Chicago and Richmond, Virginia.

Being honest though, this hypothetical city covers 570 square miles, which would make it one of the biggest cities in the U.S. (among cities over 100,000 people, outside Alaska). The city would become mostly sprawl to dilute St. Louis’s homicide rate down to still being within the top twenty most dangerous cities.

RankCityLand area
1Jacksonville747 sq. mi
2Houston641 sq. mi
3Oklahoma City607 sq. mi
4St. Louis City + County570 sq. mi
5Phoenix518 sq. mi

Where a combined St. Louis would rank by land area among U.S. cities over 100,000 people outside Alaska, 2020

It would also be the 9th largest city in the 2020 census, about the same size in population as Dallas while covering roughly 230 more square miles of land.

RankCity2020 populationLand area
7San Antonio1,434,625499 sq. mi
8San Diego1,386,932326 sq. mi
9St. Louis City + County1,305,703570 sq. mi
10Dallas1,304,379340 sq. mi

Where a combined St. Louis would rank among U.S. cities by population, 2020

Recalculating the borders does not make the dangerous parts of the city any less dangerous, and that’s a serious problem. But nonetheless, St. Louis could be viewed in a more reasonable light if it was set up in a more comparable way to other metros.

Outlook#

Reunification has been attempted several times since the split. The most recent attempt, Better Together, was withdrawn in May 2019 before it ever reached a vote.

Louisville is one of the few cities to have merged with its county, as a case study.

An actual merger has not happened in 150 years (as of this writing), and it does not seem likely. There are legitimate concerns from both sides about such an event, and the city and county finding a way to work together would not immediately fix all problems from the last 150 years, but I believe anything that could improve the city’s reputation would be a win. A more unified region could also potentially work together better to solve these issues.

St. Louis will probably not ever be the 4th largest city in the U.S. again, but if it wasn’t on the top of every “most dangerous city” list, I believe people would be more likely to visit and move here.

TL;DR#

  • St. Louis City voted to separate from St. Louis County in 1876, freezing its borders at 66 square miles.
  • The city peaked at 856,796 residents in 1950 and has shrunk every decade since, down to 301,578 in 2020. The county grew past a million during that time period.
  • Crime is measured by city boundary, so the stats cover only the urban core. St. Louis (city) had the highest 2020 murder rate (87 per 100k) of the 296 large cities reporting to the FBI. The county was estimated around 10 per 100k.
  • If the city and county were one merged city, it would be the 9th largest in the U.S. by population, roughly 4th by land area (among cities over 100,000 people outside Alaska), and its murder rate would be 28, around 15th place. This doesn’t necessarily paint the best picture, because the city would need to contain a massive amount of sprawl to bring down the statistics.
  • Reunification attempts failed in 1926, 1959, 1962, and 2019.

Sources#

Every homicide count on this page comes from a single dataset for a single year: the FBI’s official 2020 “murder and nonnegligent manslaughter” figures. Rates are those counts divided by 2020 census populations.

  • Crime in the U.S. 2020: Offenses Known to Law Enforcement - FBI Crime Data Explorer — murder counts for every reporting agency
  • QuickFacts: St. Louis city and St. Louis County - U.S. Census Bureau, 2020 populations
  • 2020 U.S. Gazetteer Files - U.S. Census Bureau — land areas
  • TIGERweb - U.S. Census Bureau — the map’s city and county boundary outlines
  • Demographics of St. Louis and St. Louis County, Missouri - census counts for the population-by-decade table

The St. Louis County total (104) is the St. Louis County Police Department (43) plus the 44 municipal police departments that reported to the FBI (61 combined). A handful of departments - Berkeley, Maryland Heights, and Webster Groves among them - did not report 2020 data, so the county figure is likely a slight undercount.

*There are 41 independent cities in the U.S. - 38 of them are in Virginia. The only ones outside it are St. Louis, Baltimore, and Carson City, Nevada.

**St. Louis’s 66 square miles includes about 4 square miles of the Mississippi River. City rankings compare land area, where the city measures 62.

item.title: Walkable Neighborhoods in St. Louis
item.description: Highlighting some of the most interesting and walkable neighborhoods to explore
item.content:encoded:
One of the first things you learn about St. Louis is there is no single main street to walk around and explore. Downtown has the Arch and the main business district, but isn’t the place most people spend their time.

St. Louis is a city of many neighborhoods, and you’ll find interesting clusters of shops and hidden gems all over the place, but it isn’t always obvious to newcomers where to look.

I’ve been on a mission to discover all these walkable spots around the city and county. A few of them are obvious - The Grove and Cherokee Street are often mentioned by name - but some I just happened to stumble upon and slowly discover over time.

To view the full combined neighborhood map, you can click here:

Explore the Neighborhood Map

Overview#

This is a map of all the walkable St. Louis streets you’ll see throughout the article.

The shaded areas denote the official neighborhoods, the lines are the highlighted streets.

Legend

  • North City neighborhood
  • Central Corridor neighborhood
  • South City neighborhood
  • St. Louis County town
  • Walkable area: the street and the places along it

Contents

  1. South City
    1. Tower Grove South
    2. Shaw
    3. Hampton & Macklind
    4. The Hill
    5. Bevo
    6. Cherokee Street
    7. Southtown
    8. Soulard
    9. Lafayette Square
    10. Carondelet
  2. Central Corridor
    1. Central West End
    2. Dogtown
    3. The Grove
    4. The Delmar Loop
  3. St. Louis County
    1. DeMun
    2. Maplewood
    3. Webster Groves
    4. Kirkwood

Central West End#

  • Street: Euclid Avenue, from Laclede to Delmar
  • Street: Maryland Plaza, from Euclid to the end of the plaza
  • Neighborhood: Central West End

Central West End is one of the most dense and urban neighborhoods outside of Downtown. Euclid is the main retail strip that runs through the neighborhood. The street is lined with large, opulent lanterns, giving the area a nice glow at night.

There are a good amount of late night food options and bars/clubs along Euclid. Tikka Tangy and Taste of Lebanon are a few of my favorite restaurants in the area. Updown, the arcade bar, is at the end of the line.

One of St. Louis’s independent bookstores, Left Bank Books, can be found here. There is also the World Chess Hall of Fame (with the world’s largest chess piece), representing St. Louis as a world chess capital.

Just off Euclid, Maryland Plaza is a short street of restaurants and boutiques around a small square, running west toward the Chase Park Plaza.

Euclid is just a few short blocks from Forest Park, the proximity of which is a huge pro for the neighborhood. It’s also a relatively bike-friendly area.

Dogtown#

  • Street: Tamm Avenue, from Oakland to Mitchell
  • Neighborhood: Dogtown

Around the Clayton and Tamm intersection in Dogtown (technically the Clayton-Tamm neighborhood) is St. Louis’s historical Irish neighborhood, where a St. Patrick’s Day parade takes place each year. There are several Irish bars in this spot, like Seamus McDaniel’s and The Pat Connolly Tavern.

Tower Grove South#

  • Street: Grand Boulevard, from Arsenal to Utah
  • Street: Morganford Road, from Arsenal to Utah
  • District: South Grand
  • Neighborhoods: Tower Grove South, Tower Grove East

South Grand is the international restaurant row of St. Louis. Along this strip, you’ll find a concentration of Vietnamese, Thai, Ethiopian, Persian, Lebanese, Indian, BBQ, and other varieties of food. Jay International Foods is also the spot to go for ingredients of the world. MoKaBe’s Coffeehouse is a popular spot for coffee.

Dunaway Books is a used book store with two floors that’s really fun to browse.

The South Grand strip stops right at Tower Grove Park, which really adds to the walkability of this street, especially on a weekend during the farmers’ market.

There’s also a smaller strip along Morganford with a few places of interest, such as Amsterdam Tavern, the soccer bar, and Songbird.

Shaw#

  • Street: South 39th Street, from Shaw to Magnolia
  • Neighborhood: Shaw

Tucked between Tower Grove Park, the Missouri Botanical Garden, and Compton Hill Park is Shaw, a quiet tree-lined neighborhood full of historical Victorian homes. This is a great area to walk due to how quiet it is, and how much green space surrounds it.

There is not exactly one main street to walk along, but several businesses dotted throughout the neighborhood. You can get pastries at Damn Fine Hand Pies, coffee at Fiddlehead Fern Cafe, and liquid-nitrogen ice cream at Ice’s Plain and Fancy.

Flora Place is a particularly pretty boulevard to walk along, showcasing many beautiful Victorian-era homes.

Hampton & Macklind#

  • Street: Hampton Avenue, from Chippewa to Gravois
  • Street: Macklind Avenue, from Lansdowne to Nottingham
  • Neighborhoods: St. Louis Hills, Southampton, Princeton Heights

Hampton Avenue around St. Louis Hills and Southampton has a very local neighborhood vibe. This is mostly a quiet area of the city with some shops, but I noticed a cluster of restaurants along the strip. There’s J.J. Twigs, a Chicago tavern-style pizza spot with the braided crust pizza, and the newly relocated Mom’s Deli, and Salvage Yard. There’s also Bono’s Pizzeria, the best Chicago deep dish I’ve had aside from Lou Malnati’s, and more restaurants I have yet to try.

There’s also another small strip nearby on Macklind with a Clementine’s ice cream shop and a few bars and restaurants. The neighborhood around the shops is also fun to walk through.

The Hill#

  • Street: Marconi Avenue, from Shaw to Elizabeth
  • Neighborhood: The Hill

The Hill is one of the most well-known neighborhoods of St. Louis. It was documented in America’s Last Little Italy: The Hill as one of the last Little Italys still around in America, and is the birthplace of the toasted ravioli, one of St. Louis’s most sacred regional foods.

St. Ambrose Church on Marconi is the heart of the neighborhood. All throughout the area, you’ll see fire hydrants and crosswalks painted in the colors of the Italian flag. You can walk around and get Italian food, sandwiches, pizza, gelato, and more.

My two favorites are Nicky Slices for Detroit-style pizza, and Pizzeria da Gloria for immaculate vibes and pizza.

Bevo#

  • Street: Gravois Avenue, from Taft to Christy
  • Neighborhood: Bevo Mill

In the ’90s, St. Louis took in many refugees from the Bosnian War, and they settled in the neighborhood of Bevo Mill. This area became known as Little Bosnia, and Gravois became the main street. For many years, Bevo had one of the largest Bosnian populations outside of Bosnia.

As far as restaurants in the area, Das Bevo is a biergarten in the Bevo windmill, which is the landmark of the neighborhood built by the Busch family back in the day. Bevo Caffe Lounge and Zlatno Zito are two spots serving traditional Balkan fare.

Although it has been thirty years since the Bosnian refugees settled in Bevo, there are still many signs of the population that built up the area. The Sebilj fountain replica stands as a monument for the region. Nowadays, much of the Bosnian population has moved to South County areas like Affton.

The Grove#

  • Street: Manchester Avenue, from the west arch to the east arch
  • District: The Grove
  • Neighborhood: Forest Park Southeast

One of the most distinctive and well-known streets in St. Louis is The Grove in Forest Park Southeast. It’s the only place that welcomes you with a lit-up neon sign from both ends so there’s no confusion about exactly where you are.

The Grove is most famous for being the city’s LGBTQ+ nightlife district. On one end, you have Platypus bar and Urban Chestnut brewery, and on the other you have Handlebar, Atomic, and Rehab. In between are a few of my favorite restaurants in the city - Sultan and The Gramophone.

The Delmar Loop#

  • Street: Delmar Boulevard, from Leland to the Pageant
  • District: Delmar Loop
  • Neighborhoods: University City, Skinker DeBaliviere, West End

In 2007, the Delmar Loop was named one of the “10 Great Streets in America” by the APA, due to the “sustained efforts of local business, government, and the community to achieve successful physical and economic revitalization”.

There are a lot of interesting things to see on the street - the St. Louis Walk of Fame stars along the sidewalk, the Pageant and Delmar Hall for concerts, Moonrise Hotel and tons of neon signs. There’s also the Loop Trolley which runs to Forest Park.

Notably, there is a concentration of very good Asian cuisine along Delmar, including my favorite ramen in the world, Kishimoto Mendo. The original Salt & Smoke BBQ and Fitz’s are here, and Vintage Vinyl is a great spot to browse for vinyl records.

Downtown#

Washington Avenue#

  • Street: Washington Avenue, from 6th to 18th
  • Neighborhood: Downtown

Washington Avenue, often referred to as Wash Ave by locals, is one of the main streets of interest in Downtown. There are a number of restaurants close to the street that serve the business district during lunch hours, such as Sugarfire BBQ and Sauce on the Side, and even the Washington Ave Food Hall.

It’s always worth mentioning City Museum, one of the most unique and interesting attractions in all of St. Louis, which is right along Wash Ave.

Being downtown, it’s as walkable as it gets, and one of the areas most likely to have a lot of foot traffic during the day.

Ballpark Village#

  • Street: Clark Avenue, from 8th to Broadway
  • Neighborhood: Downtown

Right next to Busch Stadium is Ballpark Village, a string of bars and restaurants surrounding a central entertainment district. It’s a hub for people to hang out before a ball game or concert.

Laclede’s Landing#

  • Street: North 2nd Street, from the Eads Bridge to Laclede's Landing Boulevard
  • Neighborhood: Downtown

Laclede’s Landing sits on the riverfront just north of the Arch and the Eads Bridge. It’s a few blocks of cobblestone streets and warehouses from the late 1800s, which are now restaurants and bars, and it’s the remaining piece of the city’s 19th-century commercial riverfront.

Midtown#

Grand Center#

  • Street: Grand Boulevard, from Olive to Delmar
  • Street: Washington Boulevard, from Grand to Spring
  • Neighborhood: Covenant Blu-Grand Center

Grand Center is the city’s arts district, just north of Saint Louis University. The Fabulous Fox Theatre and Powell Hall, home of the St. Louis Symphony, are on Grand, and The Sheldon, the Pulitzer Arts Foundation and the Contemporary Art Museum are a short walk west on Washington.

Midtown Alley#

  • Street: Locust Street, from Leffingwell to Theresa
  • Neighborhoods: Midtown, Covenant Blu-Grand Center

Midtown Alley is the stretch of Locust Street east of Grand that was once the city’s automotive row. Pappy’s Smokehouse is nearby.

Cherokee Street#

  • Street: Cherokee Street, from Lemp to Nebraska
  • District: Cherokee Street
  • Neighborhoods: Gravois Park, Benton Park West, Benton Park, Marine Villa

Cherokee St. is an arts district and commercial center in St. Louis. There are several restaurants, panaderias, and Mexican groceries along Cherokee. It’s the center of St. Louis’s Hispanic community, and the main area to go for good Mexican food, bakery items, and other goods. The Cinco de Mayo festival in St. Louis also happens along Cherokee.

The eastern wing of Cherokee St. is a vintage shopping district known as the antique row, with spots like Hammond’s Antiques and Books and Elder’s Antiques and a vinyl record store. This whole area is all small, family-owned storefronts with no chains and has a very eclectic, artistic vibe.

Southtown#

  • Street: South Kingshighway, from Fyler to Devonshire
  • District: Southtown
  • Neighborhoods: Bevo Mill, North Hampton, Southampton, Tower Grove South

Bud’s Pizza and Beer is one of my favorite spots for a classic slice in St. Louis, and every time I visited I noticed a couple of obelisks and signs denoting “Southtown”. Due to my research on this site, I knew Southtown was not an official St. Louis neighborhood, so I was curious.

There used to be a Southtown Famous-Barr department store at Kingshighway & Chippewa that was demolished in the ’90s that probably gave the area its name.

Now, there are new restaurants and bars filling up the space, such as the Golden Hoosier and Himalayan Yeti. It’s honestly not the most walkable area of the city due to Kingshighway being such a busy street, but I can see the area getting more and more built up as Garcia Properties is working on revitalizing it.

Soulard#

  • Street: South 12th Street, from Shenandoah to Gravois
  • Neighborhood: Soulard

I was hesitant to include Soulard in the list, because it breaks the mold by being a whole grid of bars as opposed to one main street. Nonetheless, the density of bars in the area makes it worth being included on the list of walkable neighborhoods. The majority of businesses around the area are late night and bar focused, so you won’t see much here along the lines of bookstores and cafes.

The Soulard Farmers market is one of the (if not the) oldest farmers’ markets west of the Mississippi, continuously running since 1779.

One of the largest Mardi Gras parades in the country happens in Soulard.

I haven’t spent much time in Soulard myself during its peak hours, but McGurk’s has an excellent patio. When I have driven through Soulard during the afternoon, it has felt sleepy.

The north and south ends of Soulard have a different feel, with the north side being a bit more commercial and bustling, especially with the farmers market on a Saturday morning, and the south side being more residential and quiet.

Lafayette Square#

  • Street: Park Avenue, from Mississippi to 18th
  • Neighborhood: Lafayette Square

Lafayette Park is a beautiful park in St. Louis with a pavilion, grotto, lake, and bridge. Every one of the neighborhoods on this list that borders a park gets an edge, because you can also take a stroll around the park.

There are a few notable restaurants here. Park Avenue Coffee has a location here, and it’s my absolute favorite coffee around the city (though not necessarily my favorite cafe - a few others like Telva at the Ridge, Noteworthy Cafe, etc. take the cake).

In addition to the park, there are also beautiful, historic mansions painted in vibrant colors that give this area an interesting, historic charm.

Carondelet#

  • Street: South Broadway, from Blow to Steins
  • Neighborhood: Carondelet

Carondelet is an interesting part of St. Louis that was originally its own city that was annexed by St. Louis in 1870 (one of the last that ever would be!). It’s a very old, very French village from back in the day.

I didn’t really know there was anything in Carondelet aside from Stacked (burgers) and Sugarwitch (ice cream sandwiches) but I recently discovered there’s a whole strip of bars along the riverfront. Most of St. Louis is not along the riverfront as it’s mostly been historically used for industry, so that’s kind of interesting.

DeMun#

  • Street: DeMun Avenue, from Northwood to Southwood
  • Neighborhood: Clayton

There’s a small, chic strip in Clayton right to the west of Forest Park. Concordia Park runs right along DeMun, giving you a beautiful green park to amble along after dinner and/or ice cream along the strip.

In this area, you’ll find Louie, an amazing spot to celebrate a birthday or anniversary, and Clementine’s, the St. Louis ice cream classic. A location of Sasha’s wine bar is also here, with the other being in Shaw. Many of these spots have outdoor patios, making it a lovely place to spend an evening.

DeMun is a small spot overall, but worth mentioning for how pleasant it is.

Maplewood#

  • Street: Manchester Road, from Big Bend to Bellevue
  • Neighborhood: Maplewood

In the 2010s, Maplewood was named one of the top “hipster” neighborhoods in the U.S. There’s a bit of a “Keep Maplewood Weird” vibe about the area, like a much smaller Portland or Austin.

There are two major breweries located in Maplewood - Side Project Brewing and Schlafly Bottleworks. There is also a cozy bookstore called The Book House and Strange Donuts, a local favorite donut shop. Bolyard’s Meat & Provisions is a high quality butcher in the area.

Maplewood is a streetcar suburb with MetroLink access to the city, making it one of a few. The Treasure Aisles Antique Mall is nearby, as well as some restaurants like Locoz Tacos and the Japanese Sando Shack.

Webster Groves#

  • Street: Big Bend Boulevard, from Lockwood to Oakwood
  • Street: Lockwood Avenue, from Jefferson to Maple
  • Neighborhood: Webster Groves

There are two main strips in Webster Groves. The Old Orchard district includes the famous James Beard award restaurant Balkan Treat Box and bookstore the Novel Neighbor.

There’s another main retail area with Telva at the Ridge (a cafe by the owners of Balkan Treat Box), Olive + Oak, and the Webster Groves Bookshop.

Kirkwood#

  • Street: Kirkwood Road, from Bodley to Monroe
  • Neighborhood: Kirkwood

Downtown Kirkwood is a walkable area in Kirkwood, a wealthy suburb in the county of St. Louis. There’s an Amtrak station in Kirkwood, making it more connected than most suburbs.

There are some restaurants along the main strip, like Napoli Kirkwood, Honey Bee’s Biscuits, and Billy G’s. There’s also a Strange Donuts and Clementine’s ice cream here, and notably there’s The Minifig Shop, a Lego resale store.

And of course - you guessed it - Kirkwood has a farmers market.

Conclusion#

Did I miss a few spots? Let me know! I’m still learning and exploring so there’s bound to be some areas I missed.

item.title: Where Is Dogtown? Mapping Local Names in St. Louis
item.description: How local names like Dogtown and The Grove fit onto St. Louis’s official neighborhood map
item.content:encoded:
When I first moved to St. Louis, I quickly picked up the names of various places around the city - we’d go to Seamus McDaniel’s in Dogtown, or The Gramophone in The Grove. As I explored the city more and began mapping it for this project, I discovered there are several names you won’t find on an official neighborhood map.

St. Louis has 79 official neighborhoods with clearly defined boundaries, but the way people refer to areas can be more casual. For this site, I was looking for a way to build a map that respects the official neighborhood boundaries while exposing the informal names people use as well.

Someone new to St. Louis might want to know what restaurants to check out in The Grove but not know to look in Forest Park Southeast yet. They might have been told to go check out Cherokee, which crosses multiple boundaries, or The Loop, which crosses the city-county line. And Dogtown isn’t one neighborhood, but a group of neighborhoods south of Forest Park (more on that below).

The reason I made these changes on the map is so you can view the whole map and click on related groups together, for example on a Cherokee specific page, instead of having to click between four neighborhoods to see everything on Cherokee.

Here’s a link to the full neighborhood map with restaurants, coffee shops, landmarks, museums, book and game stores, markets, parks, and write-ups. In the rest of this article, I’ll explain some of the additions and variations I made to the map.

Explore the Neighborhood Map

About the Map#

Legend

  • North City neighborhood
  • Central Corridor neighborhood
  • South City neighborhood
  • St. Louis County town
  • Park
  • District: a popular strip outlined by this site, not an official neighborhood boundary
  • Official neighborhood inside a grouped set

Mapped by one resident#

A few other cities have had surveys to crowdsource opinions about neighborhood boundaries, such as The University of Chicago’s Chicago Neighborhood Project, Chicago Neighborhoods, Mapped By Residents: Here’s Where Locals Think Official Boundaries Should Be and The New York Times An Extremely Detailed Map of New York City Neighborhoods.

I haven’t found a survey for vibes in St. Louis, maybe because the city already has legally defined boundaries. The map on this site is just one person’s attempt to create an informal map.

As a disclaimer, anything that isn’t officially defined is a matter of opinion. I am not trying to take away from the identity of any neighborhood, but just document some of what I discovered over a few years of living in, exploring, and researching St. Louis. If there’s anything I missed or got wrong, I’d love to learn about it and update the map and article!

Defining the map#

I used the map on NextSTL to first define and color code north city, south city, and the central corridor for the map.

I also wanted to include some inner-ring suburbs, as they’re a big part of the St. Louis experience. The Great Divorce prevented St. Louis from annexing its surrounding towns since the 1800s, so places like Maplewood, University City, and Clayton which might otherwise have been absorbed into the city are completely politically separate now. Nonetheless, visiting the shops and restaurants in those areas is a common experience for city residents.

On top of the official boundaries, I added two things:

  • Districts: for anything that wasn’t a full neighborhood or group of neighborhoods, such as a business strip, I overlaid a “district” boundary.
  • Grouped sets: for areas where several official neighborhoods go by one name, I combined them into one region, with a dashed line between each official neighborhood.

Districts#

Some of the most popular places to visit in St. Louis are business districts that run along a major street. In some cases, they’re contained entirely within a neighborhood’s boundaries, and in other cases they straddle the line or cross between multiple neighborhoods. Here are a few that I documented.

On this site, each place in a district is labeled with both the official neighborhood it’s in and the district it belongs to. For example, Sultan is in the neighborhood of Forest Park Southeast and the district of The Grove, and Taqueria Hectorito is in Benton Park West and the Cherokee Street district.

The districts I’ve outlined here are loosely based on what I’ve observed, but St. Louis also has Community Improvement Districts (CIDs) that inform some of these decisions. The Grove, Cherokee Street, South Grand, and the city side of the Loop each have a CID, which are used to pay for cleanup, security, events, etc. in those areas.

Here’s the map of the local taxing districts. Interestingly, a lot of the official CID boundaries overlap with my Walkable Neighborhoods in St. Louis article, such as the intersection in Dogtown, Bevo, and Southtown.

The Grove#

The Grove, famous for being St. Louis’s LGBTQ nightlife strip, is an example of a business district that is contained within a neighborhood. It runs down Manchester from Kingshighway to Vandeventer and is clearly defined by the two Grove signs on the east and west ends. The neighborhood is Forest Park Southeast.

This is also a neighborhood where the identity of the district informally extends to the whole area. Most of the homes in Forest Park Southeast are not in the Grove strip.

South Grand#

South Grand, known as St. Louis’s international dining strip, is a business district that straddles the line between Tower Grove South and Tower Grove East on S. Grand Boulevard. Which side of the street a restaurant is on determines which neighborhood it appears in.

Southtown#

Along Kingshighway in South City there’s a strip of restaurants owned by Garcia Properties, including Bud’s Pizza, The Golden Hoosier, and Uncle Bill’s Pancake House, in the area known as Southtown. There was once a department store there called Southtown Famous-Barr, which is probably where the name came from.

Cherokee Street#

Cherokee Street - part Hispanic community, part antique row - is a business district that runs through four neighborhoods: Gravois Park, Benton Park West, Benton Park, and Marine Villa. (To make things even more confusing, there’s a sign along Cherokee that says “You are in Dutchtown.” More on that in Greater Dutchtown.)

Delmar Loop#

The Delmar Loop, a major tourist attraction in St. Louis and one of the “10 Great Streets in America” according to The American Planning Association, is a business district that crosses over the city-county line. The west side is in University City, which is part of St. Louis County, and the east side is in Skinker DeBaliviere and West End, city neighborhoods.

Although the city-county line is a major division for the St. Louis region, the Loop shows that commerce easily crosses the border, connecting the two regions.

Grouped Neighborhoods#

In some instances, groups of neighborhoods are informally referred to by a single name with fuzzy boundaries. On the map, each of these is one region that encompasses the official neighborhoods, with a dashed boundary line between each one.

Dogtown#

Dogtown is the neighborhood I named this article for, as it’s the most obvious example of an informal neighborhood being formed of a grouped set of neighborhoods. There are a few community and merchant organizations all using the Dogtown name, so I’ve used the Dogtown United claim of Clayton-Tamm, Franz Park, Hi-Pointe, Cheltenham, and the eastern portion of Ellendale.

The city’s list of Community Improvement Districts even includes a Dogtown CID, though it’s marked inactive.

Source: Dogtown United: “The Dogtown area is located south of Forest Park and includes four neighborhoods of St. Louis: Clayton-Tamm, Franz Park, Hi-Pointe, Cheltenham, Ellendale (eastern portion)”.

Source: How Dogtown may have gotten its name: “If you know someone who lives in Clayton-Tamm, Franz Park, Hi-Pointe, Cheltenham or even part of Ellendale, they technically live in Dogtown, which has long been known as the Irish part of St. Louis.”

Downtown#

I’ve combined Downtown and Downtown West into a unified Downtown identity. Union Station (and the Aquarium), Energizer Park, and City Museum are all technically in Downtown West, but people just say they’re going Downtown to see a soccer game or go to the aquarium.

The urban fabric is continuous across both sides of Downtown, so I wanted to group them both together to make it easier to find related things to do.

Carondelet#

Carondelet and Patch form the southern tip of St. Louis city. Although a large portion of the restaurants and bars are actually located in Patch, the whole area is often informally called Carondelet. Stacked Burger Bar refers to their Carondelet location despite it being in Patch, for example, and Sauce Magazine groups everything under Carondelet/S. Broadway.

The whole area used to be called Carondelet and was its own independent city separate from St. Louis until 1870. A century later in 1971 it was split into the two neighborhoods of Carondelet and Patch. This history has resulted in a lot of shared identity between the two neighborhoods.

The last 50 years have surely made the two areas distinct to the residents that live there, but for the purposes of my map I am grouping them together for all the restaurants, breweries, and bars.

Source: Patch, St. Louis on Wikipedia: “The Patch neighborhood forms the southern tip of the Carondelet neighborhood”.

Source: St. Louis City Talk: “First of all I always thought this area was Carondelet. Live and learn…this is Patch, the neighborhood with the coolest name of all 79.”

Source: St. Louis Patina: “An eclectic area of South City, the official City of St. Louis neighborhood name for this area is Patch. However, many people I talk to simply consider this Carondelet, if the very southern tip of it.”

Groupings Not on the Map#

A couple of other groupings came up while I was mapping, but I left the neighborhoods independent on the map.

Greater Dutchtown#

Dutchtown is a neighborhood in South City. A few neighborhood organizations such as DutchtownSTL.org and Dutchtown South Community Corporation include the four neighborhoods of Gravois Park, Mount Pleasant, Marine Villa, and Dutchtown itself within their purview.

While walking along Cherokee Street, I noticed a sign that said “You are in Dutchtown”, a nod to how some local groups use the Dutchtown name for the wider area beyond its official bounds.

Personally, I haven’t explored these neighborhoods too much yet, so it’s easy for me to group them all together, but people who live there have stronger opinions. Since I had pushback, I just left all the neighborhoods on the map independent, but wanted to include it in this article for completeness.

Source: DutchtownSTL.org: “The boundaries of what’s generally referred to as “Dutchtown” are quite fuzzy. The City of St. Louis defines some very specific boundaries. But signs around the neighborhood will tell you that “You Are In Dutchtown” when you are, in fact, in Gravois Park, Mount Pleasant, or Marine Villa. Here at DutchtownSTL, we approximate Dutchtown to be everything in between Cherokee Street or Chippewa Street to the north, Bates Street to the south, the Mississippi River to the east, and the Missouri Pacific railroad tracks to the west.”

Source: Dutchtown South Community Corporation: “Dutchtown South Community Corporation supports four vibrant neighborhoods in South St. Louis City: Dutchtown, Gravois Park, Marine Villa, Mt. Pleasant.”

Midtown#

Between Midtown, Central West End, and Grand Center, places sometimes all get grouped into Midtown. For example, The Cortex is mostly in Central West End and the Fabulous Fox is in Grand Center, but I’ve heard both referred to as being in Midtown before.

Known by Official Names#

Many other popular neighborhoods in the city are known by their official name. The Hill, Soulard, Lafayette Square, Shaw, and Central West End are all official names. Some are shortened slightly, as people often call Bevo Mill simply Bevo, or Covenant Blu-Grand Center as just Grand Center.

Official names can change, too. Botanical Heights was called McRee Town until it was renamed as part of a redevelopment plan in the early 2000s.

Source: Missouri Historical Society, Gerard Connolly Collection: McRee Town was renamed Botanical Heights as part of a rehabilitation plan.

St. Louis County#

The different areas of the county are loosely grouped together as North County, West County, and South County, and often colloquially referred to with those names.

I included University City, Clayton, Maplewood, Richmond Heights, Affton, Kirkwood, and a few other towns on the map. If you’re going on a St. Louis-style pizza tour, for example, you should go way north to Pirrone’s and way west to Faraci’s, both of which aren’t located in the city.

I still have a lot of work to do to complete all the write-ups and exploration of the county.

Conclusion#

In summary:

  • places like The Grove, Cherokee, and Delmar Loop aren’t neighborhoods, so I outlined them as districts that can be searched by name
  • places like Dogtown are not officially defined, but rather a group of neighborhoods under one colloquial name
  • most other neighborhoods go by their official names, sometimes shortened
  • the map extends into inner-ring suburbs in St. Louis County, because the culture of the region crosses the city-county line

It has been a fun project for me as a transplant to map St. Louis and keep exploring and taking pictures and trying new food, and I hope it’s useful or interesting to others as well. item.title: Southtown
item.description: Bud's Pizza and Beer is one of my favorite spots for a classic slice in St. Louis, and every time I visited I noticed a couple of obelisks and signs denoting…
item.content:encoded:
Bud’s Pizza and Beer is one of my favorite spots for a classic slice in St. Louis, and every time I visited I noticed a couple of obelisks and signs denoting “Southtown”. Due to my research on this site, I knew Southtown was not an official St. Louis neighborhood, so I was curious.

There used to be a Southtown Famous-Barr department store at Kingshighway & Chippewa that was demolished in the ’90s that gave the area its name.

Now, there are new restaurants and bars filling up the space, such as the Golden Hoosier and Himalayan Yeti. It’s honestly not the most walkable area of the city due to Kingshighway being such a busy street, but I can see the area getting more and more built up as Garcia Properties is working on revitalizing it.

item.title: South Grand
item.description: South Grand is a business district just south of Tower Grove Park with six blocks of international dining options and small, independent businesses. It sits on…
item.content:encoded:
South Grand is a business district just south of Tower Grove Park with six blocks of international dining options and small, independent businesses.

It sits on the line between Tower Grove South and Tower Grove East. Along this strip you’ll find a concentrated variety of restaurants, from Persian, Lebanese, and Turkish to pizza, hot dogs, and cafes.

There are also some small, independent stores such as Dunaway Books, Apotheosis Comics, and Circa: Now! Records, which all together make this a good area for walking, shopping and eating.

item.title: Good Strangers
item.description: Near the corner of Cherokee St. and Jefferson Ave. you'll find Good Strangers, a cafe serving up unique lattes and small bites. It sits right at the dividing…
item.content:encoded:
Near the corner of Cherokee St. and Jefferson Ave. you’ll find Good Strangers, a cafe serving up unique lattes and small bites. It sits right at the dividing line between the west side of Cherokee St., which is full of Mexican grocery stores, taquerias, and panaderias, and the east side, which is the historic Cherokee Antique Row.

Good Strangers advertise themselves as “Midwest Tex-Mexiterrean” which is likely a brand-new genre of food, but I’m into it. The vibes inside the store are very welcoming and vibrant when I visited on a Saturday afternoon.

The cafe opened in 2020 according to the sign near their menu (“Seemed like a good idea at the time”), so I’m glad to see they weathered the pandemic storm and made it through the other side. I enjoyed hanging out here for a bit before exploring Cherokee.

It also looks like a yarn store operates out of the building, which adds to the comforting ambience.

item.title: Cherokee Street
item.description: Cherokee St. is an arts district and commercial center in St. Louis. Along the western side of the street are several restaurants, panaderias, and Mexican…
item.content:encoded:
Cherokee St. is an arts district and commercial center in St. Louis. Along the western side of the street are several restaurants, panaderias, and Mexican groceries along Cherokee. It’s the center of St. Louis’s Hispanic community, and the main area to go for good Mexican food and pastries. The Cinco de Mayo festival in St. Louis also happens along Cherokee.

The eastern wing of Cherokee St. is a vintage shopping district known as the antique row, with spots like Hammond’s Antiques and Books and Elder’s Antiques and a vinyl record store. This whole area is all small, family-owned storefronts with no chains and has a very eclectic, artistic vibe.

In the middle near Jefferson you’ll find a few hidden gem cafes and bakeries, like Good Strangers.

item.title: Napoli Kirkwood
item.description: I thought Napoli at Kirkwood was okay. It's nice that there's an outdoor patio, but it's right along an extremely loud and busy street, so it doesn't have the…
item.content:encoded: I thought Napoli at Kirkwood was okay. It’s nice that there’s an outdoor patio, but it’s right along an extremely loud and busy street, so it doesn’t have the best ambience. They don’t make their own toasted ravioli, which I expected because they make some of their own pasta. Since it’s a bigger location it might be good for a big group, but I’d rather go to Louie or Pizzeria da Gloria or some other Italian places.

item.title: Taqueria El Bronco
item.description: I've been on the lookout for a particular type of burrito - grilled steak, with lettuce, tomato, sour cream, queso fresco, and refried beans, on a griddled…
item.content:encoded: I’ve been on the lookout for a particular type of burrito - grilled steak, with lettuce, tomato, sour cream, queso fresco, and refried beans, on a griddled tortilla. Taqueria El Bronco is one of the first spots I tried to find this, but it didn’t hit for me so I haven’t been back since. I’m sure there’s something else on the menu that is much better, so I’m planning to go back and give it another shot at some point.

item.title: Dutchtown
item.description: Dutchtown is one of the most densely populated areas of St. Louis city. The area was originally populated by German immigrants in late nineteenth century,…
item.content:encoded:
Dutchtown is one of the most densely populated areas of St. Louis city.

The area was originally populated by German immigrants in late nineteenth century, which is where the name Dutchtown (Deutschtown) originated. Currently, it is one of the more diverse neighborhoods in South City, with a significant Black and Hispanic population.

Dutchtown Proud is the motto of this neighborhood, and you’ll see “Dutchtown Proud” signs in yards all around. A lot of people clearly take pride in the neighborhood are putting in a lot of work to make Dutchtown a good place to live, work, and visit.

item.title: Grand Pied
item.description: On the northwest side of the Tower Grove South community, there's a strip of restaurants, cafes and businesses along Morganford Rd. One of these is Grand Pied,…
item.content:encoded:
On the northwest side of the Tower Grove South community, there’s a strip of restaurants, cafes and businesses along Morganford Rd. One of these is Grand Pied, which is French for “Bigfoot”.

I was looking for a good breakfast and I had heard about Grand Pied and their famous pancakes, so I went to go check it out. If anything, the pancakes were undersold, as after the first bite I was sure they were easily the best pancakes I’ve ever had in my life. Generally, I’m not into pancakes but these were crispy on the outside and perfectly fluffy on the inside. They come with (real) Maple syrup, blackberry jam, homemade whipped cream and butter.

I ordered the “kid’s pancakes” to get all the toppings on the side, as I wanted to keep it as crisp as possible and play around with the portions of toppings. All of them were very high quality. (I think calling the exact same dish “kid’s pancakes” and charging more for them is a weirdly passive-aggressive way to try to get people not to order toppings on the side, but whatever).

We also got beignets, which were pretty good but not the softest, lightest ones I’ve ever had, and not the main attraction here. If you’re going to get fried dough at Grand Pied, make it the pancakes.

The coffee and cold brew were both really good. I tend to not like coffee from more upscale brunch spots as it tends to be very acidic, but this coffee was from Dubuque and was well-rounded. My only complaint about my entire stay at Grand Pied was that the coffee was “bottomless” but no one ever came around to refill it or check on us during our stay, as it’s a QR-code based ordering system.

The ambience of the restaurant had a lot of character with the mural on the wall and various paintings and decorations. The coffee was served in a mug which was a nice touch, and the flowers added a lot of brightness to the room. There was also a patio outside with a lot of greenery which added to the vibe.

I’d consider Grand Pied to be an absolute must-try, especially for anyone who is a fan of pancakes. I’ll be going back to try some of the other food.
